   CITY OF BEVERLY HILLS

  PUBLIC WORKS DEPARTMENT

  MEMORANDUM

 TO:  City Council / Public Works Commission Liaison Committee
 FROM:  Teresa Revis, Associate Project Manager
  Ken Pfalzgraf, City Arborist
 DATE:  August 12, 2026
 SUBJECT:  Coldwater Cañon Street Tree Master Plan

 ATTACHMENT:  1. July 17, 2025, Public Works Commission Report, Coldwater Cañon
  Street Tree Master Plan Update
  2. March 13, 2025, Public Works Commission Report, Coldwater
  Canyon Pine Tree Assessment
  3. Ballot Package

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends that the Liaison:
  1. Accept the staff and Public Works Commission recommendation to use Chinese Pistache
  trees — selected through a vote by Coldwater Cañon Drive property owners — to fill
  vacant tree sites and to replace Canary Island Pines only as they are lost.
  2. Support the recommendation for City Council consideration and approval.

INTRODUCTION

At the June 11, 2026, Public Works Commission Meeting, the Commission reviewed the results
of the public process of selecting an updated Street Tree Master Plan for Coldwater Cañon Drive.
At this time, staff seeks support from the City Council / Public Works Commission Liaison
Committee (Liaison) for a Street Tree Master Plan to replace the Canary Island Pine Trees on
Coldwater Cañon Drive with the Chinese Pistache tree selected by the largest share of
responding property owners. This project was initiated by staff to determine an appropriate
replacement tree and address the increasing tree vacancies on the street. If approved, the
Chinese Pistache tree will only be used to fill existing vacant tree locations and as Canary Island
Pines fail in the future.

BACKGROUND

The Canary Island Pine (Pinus canariensis) trees along Coldwater Cañon Drive are approximately
75 years old. Since the time of their planting, several factors have diminished the long-term
performance of the trees, mainly the activity of boring insects and drought conditions. The area
of the City north of Sunset Boulevard is designated as a Very High Fire Hazard Severity Zone
(VHFHSZ). Canary Island Pines are undesirable for planting on both public and private property
in a VHFHSZ because they drop thick, dry needles that burn fast; additionally, the Fire Department
has requested increased spacing of street trees in the VHFHSZ to reduce the risk of high intensity
crown fires that spread from tree to tree.
 Due to these significant concerns, the Canary Island Pine is not sustainable as a street tree in the
City of Beverly Hills. At present there are approximately 50 vacant tree sites on Coldwater Cañon
Drive.

During the March 13, 2025, Public Works Commission meeting, the Commission supported a staff
recommendation that a Street Tree Master Plan (STMP) phase, which includes the identification
of possible new tree types to be used when Canary Island Pines are lost, be developed for
Coldwater Cañon Drive. On Sunday, May 18, 2025, staff, along with Commissioner Mark
Nehoray, Public Works Commission Coldwater Street Tree Master Plan Ad Hoc Committee met
on the street with residents to discuss the declining pine trees, observe the problematic
conditions, and review alternative trees, which were available to view in 36-inch box size samples.
After the meeting, staff returned to the Public Works Commission on July 17, 2025, and received
direction to move forward with presenting the options in a ballot to all property owners on
Coldwater Cañon Drive.

The Street Tree Master Plan Process is outlined in the City of Beverly Hills Street Tree Master
Plan Focused Study dated November 26, 1996, and its associated resolution 96-R-2525.

The selection of a replacement tree includes extensive knowledge of trees, our specific
environment and horticultural needs and restrictions. Some of the factors that are included in the
selection are:
  1. Is the tree appropriate to the growspace (e.g. parkway width, aerial setbacks)?
  2. Does the tree have a proven performance record in the City of Beverly Hills or in a similar
  climate with similar growing conditions?
  3. Does the tree pose toxicity or allergen concerns to the public?
  4. Is the tree appropriate to low water availability issues or drought?
  5. Will the tree complement the increased canopy coverage goals of the Urban Forest
  Management Plan?
  6. Will the tree significantly increase maintenance costs, to include costs related to private
  property maintenance and/or long-term City infrastructure repairs?
  7. Is the tree type locally available in the size, quantity and condition appropriate for the
  current and future needs of the project?

Staff mailed a ballot to the owners of the 67 properties on Coldwater Cañon on October 3, 2025.
The ballot offered four choices:

  1.  No replacement (leave existing and future tree vacancies empty)
  2.  Replace with Chinese Pistache (Pistacia chinensis), a colorful deciduous tree
  3.  Replace with Holly Oak (Quercus ilex), an evergreen tree
  4.  Replace with Sky Climber Oak (Quercus virginiana ‘Sky Climber’), a semi-deciduous
  variety of Southern Live Oak

Information sheets for each of the proposed tree types were mailed to each property owner with
each ballot.

DISCUSSION

Staff sent ballots to the property owners on October 3, 2025. When this initial ballot failed to gain
a majority, staff sent subsequent ballots to the remaining properties on November 18, 2025,

  2 of 3
 January 6, 2026, March 2, 2026, and May 14, 2026, with a total of 247 ballots mailed to the owners
across the five rounds.

Of the 67 properties, the City has now received 43 responses (64%). Six (6) of these responses
requested no change and 37 responses selected a replacement tree (55%), meeting the minimum
goal of over 50% positive response.

The responses are summarized in the table below:

  Ballot selection  Votes  Percent of positive  Percent of all
  responses (37)  properties (67)
  Chinese Pistache  21  57%  31%
  Holly Oak  12  32%  18%
  Sky Climber Oak  4  11%  6%
  Total selecting a replacement  37  100%  55%
  No change  6  —  9%
  Total overall responses  43  —  64%

Among owners who expressed a species preference, the Chinese Pistache was the clear choice,
and because it will be used only to fill vacancies and replace pines as they are lost, no healthy
tree is removed to plant one.

As previously stated, there are approximately 50 vacant tree sites currently on Coldwater Cañon.
The remaining Canary Island Pine trees will continue on their existing maintenance plan and will
continue to be evaluated through the Urban Forestry Division and will be kept in place as long as
they are healthy.

The removal and replacement of Canary Island Pines on Coldwater Cañon Drive would only occur
under the following conditions:
  1. A site is currently vacant
  2. A tree is standing dead
  3. A tree is damaged (i.e. storm, vehicle impact) to the point where it poses a danger to the
  public
  4. A tree is destabilized by root-pruning during a construction project to the point where it is
  potentially unstable and/or presents a danger to the public.
On June 11, 2026, staff presented the results of the ballot to the Public Works Commission. Four
public comments were received and read into the record, all stating that they did not agree with
the Chinese Pistache tree as a replacement. The Commission approved the recommendation by
3-to-1 vote (one Commissioner was not in attendance). One Commissioner dissented, citing the
low response rate (43 of 67 properties) and the fact that only 31% of all property owners selected
the Chinese Pistache, and advocated for an additional ballot round before proceeding.

FISCAL IMPACT

The cost for purchase and installation of each tree is approximately $2,000 or $100,000 for the
50 currently vacant spaces which is within the existing Street Tree Master Plan budget. Any future
removals would occur only under the conditions above and would be budgeted as needed in
subsequent years.

   CITY OF BEVERLY HILLS

  PUBLIC WORKS DEPARTMENT

  MEMORANDUM

TO:  Public Works Commission

FROM:  Ken Pfalzgraf, City Arborist

DATE:  July 17, 2025

SUBJECT:  Coldwater Cañon Street Tree Master Plan Update

ATTACHMENTS:  1.  March 13, 2025 Coldwater Cañon Drive Staff Report to PWC
  2.  Onsite Meeting Notice to Coldwater Cañon Drive Property Owners
  3.  Tree Information Sheets for Potential New Tree Types
  4.  Sample Ballot Form for Coldwater Cañon Drive STMP Project

INTRODUCTION
At this time, staff seeks the support of the Commission in surveying the property owners of
Coldwater Cañon Drive to select a new tree type to be used to fill currently vacant City tree
sites and to be used as Canary Island Pine trees are lost in the future.

BACKGROUND
Information regarding the historical performance of Canary Island Pines on Coldwater Cañon
Drive, as well as its undesirability in Very High Fire Hazard Severity Zones is provided in the
staff report to the Commission dated March 13, 2025 (Attachment 1).

During the March 13, 2025 meeting, the Commission supported the staff recommendation to
develop a Street Tree Master Plan (STMP) for Coldwater Cañon Drive. This phase would
identify new tree types to replace Canary Island Pines as they are lost. Staff suggested
beginning the process with an onsite meeting where residents could observe and discuss
problematic conditions firsthand, as well as view and evaluate potential new tree candidates.
Following input from residents who attend the street meeting, the Commission would determine
next steps for developing the STMP phase for this street.

DISCUSSION
After noticing residents of the street (Attachment 2), the onsite meeting was held on Coldwater
Cañon Drive on Sunday May 18, 2025. The meeting was attended by four residents from
different addresses, representing approximately 5.8% of Coldwater addresses (4 out of 69 total
addresses on the street). Staff was joined by a member of the Public Works Commission Street
Tree Master Plan Ad Hoc Committee.

The meeting began with a discussion of data regarding the pine trees' performance since their
planting in the 1950s. All of the attendees expressed a high value for the existing pines. The
group then discussed three types of trees recommended by the City Arborist as appropriate
candidates to fill currently vacant tree sites and to serve as replacements as pines on the street
are lost in the future (Attachment 3). The City Arborist advised attendees that each of the trees
being displayed on the street in 36 inch box-sized samples, meet the criteria set forth by the
 Public Works Commission for the consideration of replacement tree candidates fin the
development of a STMP phase. That criteria includes:

  •  Is the tree appropriate to the growspace (e.g. parkway width, aerial setbacks)?
  •  Does the tree have a proven performance record in the City of Beverly Hills or in a
  similar climate with similar growing conditions?
  •  Does the tree pose toxicity or allergen concerns to the public?
  •  Is the tree appropriate to low water availability issues or drought?
  •  Will the tree complement the increased canopy coverage goals of the Urban Forest
  Management Plan?
  •  Will the tree significantly increase maintenance costs, to include costs related to private
  property maintenance and/or long-term City infrastructure repairs?
  •  Is the tree type locally available in the size, quantity and condition appropriate for the
  current and future needs of the project?

In addition to being able to see physical samples of the nursery stock available for the
recommended tree types, the attendees were provided with tree information sheets (see
attached) for each of the proposed tree types, which are:

  •  Chinese Pistache (Pistache chinensis), a colorful deciduous tree
  •  Holly Oak (Quercus ilex), an evergreen tree
  •  Sky Climber Oak (Quercus virginiana ‘Sky Climber’), a semi-deciduous variety of
  Southern Live Oak

At the close of the May 18, 2025 onsite meeting, the group generally agreed that the tree
species that loses all its leaves annually was not appealing, but found one of the oak varieties
more acceptable. However, some attendees indicated a preference to not replace the pines with
any other tree type.

NEXT STEPS
Staff suggests that the Commission considers the input of the ad hoc and public comment prior
to supporting the staff recommendation to ballot the residents of the street to choose a tree type
to fill current and future vacancies on Coldwater Cañon Drive.

A sample of the balloting form is included as Attachment 4. The ballot allows the respondent to
choose between making no change and leaving lost pine sites vacant and choosing one of the
recommended tree types chosen by majority vote.

When 51% or more of the addresses on the street respond to the ballot, staff will return to the
Commission to seek the approval of the new tree type. Once the STMP phase for Coldwater
Cañon Drive is approved by the Commission, staff will seek City Council approval for the
project.

   CITY OF BEVERLY HILLS

  PUBLIC WORKS DEPARTMENT

  MEMORANDUM

 TO:  Public Works Commission
 FROM:  Ken Pfalzgraf, City Arborist

 DATE:  March 13, 2025
 SUBJECT:  Coldwater Canyon Pine Tree Assessment

 ATTACHMENT:  1. Public Notice of Coldwater Trees Discussion at Mach 13, 2025
  Public Works Commission Meeting

INTRODUCTION
At this time, staff seeks input from the Commission in the public outreach process to
choose an appropriate tree to replace Canary Island Pines on Coldwater Canyon as they
are lost in the future.

The Canary Island Pine (Pinus canariensis) trees that line Coldwater Canyon Drive are
approximately 75 years old. Over the history of the population, several factors have
diminished the long-term performance of the trees; mainly the activity of boring insects
and drought conditions. Since the northern part of the City was declared a High Severity
Fire Zone (HSFZ) several years ago, the Coldwater pines have joined the list of trees that
are undesirable for planting on both public and private property. Furthermore, the City’s
Fire Department has suggested that increasing the spacing of street trees in the HSFZ
would reduce the risk of high intensity crown fires that spread from tree to tree.

An ongoing infrastructure repair project that will replace some curbs, drive aprons and
sidewalks in the vicinity of some trees will further impact the health and longevity of the
tree population. The project will include the repair of infrastructure that has been
damaged or displaced by the roots of the trees. The level of root cutting necessary to
effect the repairs will be significant enough that the stability of some trees will come into
question. Root cutting will also decrease the ability of trees to hydrate themselves,
making them increasingly susceptible to boring insect attack in the future.

In summary, due to several significant concerns, the Canary Island Pine is not sustainable
as a street tree in the City of Beverly Hills.

BACKGROUND
The history of the Beverly Hills street tree population is summarized in the Street Tree
Plan documents of 1944, 1957 and 1963. Within the 160 projects listed within those
documents, the only reference to the Coldwater Canary Island Pines is an inventory listing
showing that there were 262 trees. Real estate listings suggest that the majority of the
residential homes along Coldwater were built in the 1950’s, meaning that the street tree
 plantings were relatively young when they were listed in the 1963 Street Tree document.
The original plantings are now approximately 75 years old.

The City completed its online inventory of public trees in 2001, about the time the
Coldwater pines had been in the ground for 50 years. In addition to providing information
about the current number of trees and their sizes, the inventory maintains work history
records for each tree in the inventory.

The work records for the Coldwater pines show that, in the last 20 years, approximately
a third of the original trees have been lost, mainly due to the activity of bark beetles that
attack drought stressed trees. A small percentage of the trees (approximately two
percent) required removal due to potential instability related to construction activity
necessary to repair infrastructure damage caused by the trees.

Typically, one tree is lost to the activity of the beetle, then over a period of three to five
years, other adjacent trees are lost to localized beetle activity. The loss of trees to beetles
tends to be in clusters, which leaves holes in the canopy and new wind exposures to trees
that had enjoyed the protection from wind that neighboring trees offered in the past. The
resulting twisting and failing limbs create wounds that provide new feeding sites for the
ever-present bark beetles. The historic trendline shows that an increasing number of
trees will be lost to beetles and drought in the future. At present, there are 39 vacant sites
waiting to be planted.

DISCUSSION
Future use of Canary Island Pine as a street tree in Beverly Hills: Using Canary Island
Pine as a replacement tree when losses are incurred has proven marginally successful,
with inventory records showing that 47 percent of the replacement sites failing within the
first 10 years after replanting. Increasing temperatures, coupled with higher water costs,
make it increasingly clear that the Canary Island Pine is not sustainable as the street tree
for Coldwater Canyon Drive.

A recent third party study of the City’s Urban Forest (Dudek’s Urban Forest Management
Plan or UFMP) concluded that several currently used street tree types are not suitable for
the higher temperatures and decreased rainfall that are anticipated for the future. Canary
Island Pine was among those tree types identified in the report.

Finally, the City Fire Department has listed a number of tree types that are not suitable
for planting in High Severity Fire Zones (HSFZ); Canary Island Pine is included in the list.

In summary, Canary Island Pine is not a sustainable tree for use in the future in the City
of Beverly Hills.

Replacement of Canary Island Pine trees: Staff suggests that the removal and
replacement of Canary Island Pines on Coldwater occurs only under the following
conditions:
  1. A tree is standing dead

  2 of 4
   2. A tree is damaged (i.e. storm, vehicle impact) to the point where it poses a danger
  to the public
  3. A tree is destabilized during a construction project to the point where it is potentially
  unstable and/or presents a danger to the public.

Choice of replacement tree type: the replacement of a tree on a City street requires the
development of a Street Tree Master Plan phase, if the type of tree being planted is a
change from what has historically lined the street. In addition, the balloting process for
the selection of a new tree type must be responded to by more than 50% of the affected
addresses for a recommendation to move forward to the Public Works Commission, and
then on for consideration by the City Council.

With the Canary Island Pine not being appropriate for future planting on Coldwater
Canyon, the selection of replacement tree candidates will include the following criteria:

  •  Is the tree appropriate to the growspace (e.g. parkway width, aerial setbacks)?
  •  Does the tree have a proven performance record in the City of Beverly Hills or in
  a similar climate with similar growing conditions?
  •  Does the tree pose toxicity or allergen concerns to the public?
  •  Is the tree appropriate to low water availability issues or drought?
  •  Will the tree compliment the increased canopy coverage goals of the Urban Forest
  Management Plan?
  •  Will the tree significantly increase maintenance costs, to include costs related to
  private property maintenance and/or long-term City infrastructure repairs?
  •  Is the tree type locally available in the size, quantity and condition appropriate for
  the current and future needs of the project?

These considerations must be included in any staff report that is presented to the Public
Works Commission prior to consideration by the City Council.

In March of 2024, staff met with the Public Works Commission Street Tree Master Plan
ad hoc on Coldwater Canyon Drive near Cabrillo Reservoir. The discussion began with
a review of how the historic data is displayed in the performance of the trees in the field.
In addition, consideration was given to the Fire Department’s position that conifers are
not desirable in the High Severity Fire Zone, meaning that an alternative tree type would
need to be chosen to fill current and future vacancies as further attrition is experienced in
the pines.

In summary, given the inappropriateness of the Canary Island Pine in the HSFZ, staff
recommends developing a Street Tree Master Plan phase for Coldwater Canyon to
consider a replacement tree type and appropriate spacing at planting to compliment Fire
Department mitigation efforts.

NEXT STEPS
Staff has noticed property owners on Coldwater Canyon that a discussion regarding the
Coldwater pine street trees will be on the agenda for the March 13, 2025 Public Works

  Chinese Pistache (Pistacia chinensis)

  *36” box Chinese Pistache

  Moderate-aged Chinese Pistache-Santa Clarita, CA  Chinese Pistache leaves-fall color

The Chinese Pistache is a moderate sized deciduous tree with a broad oval crown at
maturity when it can be 40 feet tall and nearly as wide. The deep green lance-shaped
leaves can be up to 10 inches long and are arranged in an alternating pattern. Before
dropping to the ground in late fall, the leaves turn brilliant red. Male trees produce no
fruit. Pruning requirements are minimal, once the structure of young trees is established
though train pruning to develop a strong central leader. The tree tolerates different soil
types and is known to be a low water user once established.

The Chinese Pistache is available in 36-inch box size containers. At the time of
installation, a 36-inch box tree would be approximately 10 feet tall, with a crown spread
of approximately 5 feet.

The Chinese Pistache will be a new introduction into the Beverly Hills street tree
inventory.

  Holly Oak (Quercus ilex)

  *36” box Holly Oak

  Moderate-age Holly Oak-Santa Clarita, CA  Holly Oak-leaves/acorns

Native to the Mediterranean region, the Holly Oak is a slow growing, evergreen tree.
The crown of the Holly Oak is rounded in youth, growing more open as it matures. The
tree reaches a height of 50 feet or more at maturity. The Holly Oak is a good choice for
a street tree due to its medium size fit to a narrower setback. The1.5-3-inch leaves are
lance shaped with toothed margins, glossy green above and whitish below. The
inconspicuous flower clusters develop into rounded 1-inch acorns. The blackish gray
bark appears as a collection of furrowed squares. The tree is generally pest and
disease free. Holly Oaks require train pruning when young but require minimal pruning
with age.

The Holly Oak is available in 36-inch box size containers. At the time of installation, a
36-inch box tree would be approximately 10 feet tall, with a crown spread of
approximately 5 feet.

Mature Holly Oaks can be found on Elevado Avenue.

  Sky Climber Live Oak (Quercus virginiana)

  *36” box Sky Climber Oak

  Moderate size Live Oak-Greystone Mansion  Live Oak-leaves

The Sky Climber Live Oak is a hybrid of Southern Live Oak, which is native to the
southeastern United States. This oak is partially deciduous, with a moderate growth
rate. The crown tends to be dense and pyramidal, growing to heights in excess of 60
feet at maturity. Its consistent upright growth habit makes it a good street tree. The 3-
inch-long leaves are lance-shaped, glossy green on the upper side and yellowish below
The inconspicuous flower clusters develop into rounded 3/4-inch acorns. The blackish
gray bark appears as a collection of furrowed squares as the tree ages. The tree is
generally pest and disease free.  Live Oaks require train pruning when young but
require minimal pruning with age. The Sky Climber Live Oak is characterized as a low
water user once established.

The Sky Climber Live Oak is available in 36-inch box size containers. At the time of
installation, a 36-inch box tree would be approximately 10 feet tall, with a crown spread
of approximately 5 feet.

Southern Live Oaks are located on Doheny Road to the south of Greystone Mansion
and in the Beverly Hills Community Dog Park.
